name: Nahuatl
summary: A Uto-Aztecan language of central Mexico, heir to Classical Nahuatl. Its speakers call it maseuallâjtolli; it is also known as Mexicano or Central Nahuatl.

conjugator.label: Verb
conjugator.hint: Type the verb as in the dictionary, with its object: tlachiua «make, do», tlâjtoa «speak», kochi «sleep». If you type ki- (kichiua), it is conjugated with «it». The circumflex is optional.

own.hint: Type the root of any verb, its meaning in English and whether it takes an object. We conjugate it with the rules of Central Nahuatl.
own.label: Verb root
own.types_help: If it takes ki-, write the meaning with «it»: «do it». The past-tense class is worked out from the shape of the root.

source.full: Thelma D. Sullivan, Compendio de la gramática náhuatl (UNAM, Instituto de Investigaciones Históricas); David Charles Wright Carr, Lectura del náhuatl, revised and expanded edition (INALI, 2016). Spelling: Tlâjkuilolpamitl (SEP), following Sun's Nahuatl course.

about: Nahuatl is a Uto-Aztecan language spoken by about one and a half million people in Mexico. Central Nahuatl (NHN) is spoken in parts of Milpa Alta, Tláhuac and Texcoco, in the Valley of Mexico.
Maseuallâjtolli means «the language of the common people»: maseualli «person of the town» and tlajtolli «word, language».

«Classical» Nahuatl, the language of the texts from the 16th to the 18th century, is not a different language: it is the oldest recorded stage of the central varieties. That is why this conjugator follows the grammars of Classical Nahuatl and writes them with today's spelling.

orthography.intro: We use Tlâjkuilolpamitl, the SEP spelling: 4 vowels and 14 consonants. J is the glottal stop, u sounds like w, and the circumflex (â, ê, î, ô) marks a vowel that absorbed another when two words joined.
notes: The circumflex doesn't change the sound: it shows that this vowel absorbed another when the word was formed. No + iknitl → nôkniu «my brother»; tla + ijtoa → tlâjtoa «speak».
U is always a consonant, like w: uakax, siuatl. Ku is read [kʷ]: kualli «good».
Pronunciation is shown in brackets with the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA).

grammar.intro: A Nahuatl verb is built with prefixes and suffixes around the root: who does it, to whom, when and how many.

items.description: ni- I, ti- you or we, an- you all.

blocks.title: Subject and object prefixes
blocks.description: The 3rd person has no subject prefix. Ti- is «you» or «we»: the plural has -j at the end.
blocks.note: Ki- becomes k- after a vowel: ni + ki + chiua → nikchiua.

blocks.title: Four classes of verbs in the past
blocks.description: Each verb makes its past in one of four ways. All of them start with o-.

items.name: Adds -k
items.description: Verbs that end in two consonants + vowel, and a few others.

items.name: Drops the last vowel
items.description: The most common class. A final m becomes n.

items.name: -ia, -oa → -j
items.description: They drop the final a and add -j.

blocks.title: Vowels that merge
blocks.description: When a prefix ending in a vowel meets a verb that starts with i, the i disappears and the other vowel takes a circumflex.

blocks.title: The moods
blocks.description: With ma you ask for things; with xi- you give an order to «you» or «you all»; amo negates.

tenses.name: Optative
tenses.description: Orders and wishes: xi- for you and you all, ma for the others.

tenses.name: Going to
tenses.description: Going with the purpose of doing it (-tiu; plural -tin).

tenses.name: Went to
tenses.description: Went with the purpose of doing it (o- … -to; plural -ton).
